turns.answer:
Not a dumb question — and no, the guidance says not to do that. You should never insert the electrode into a stock buffer bottle: "Do not insert an electrode or other material into a bottle containing stock buffer solution—always pour the buffer into a separate container and discard the solution after use" 【6】. The reason given is contamination — a wet or contaminated electrode placed into the solution can contaminate or dilute it 【6】.

Instead, pour the buffer into a separate, dedicated beaker for calibration 【3】, and rinse the electrode with the buffer before measuring 【6】. Also note buffers that have been poured out shouldn't go back — they're discarded after use 【6】.

3.0 	Maintenance and Preparation of
pH Instruments
Proper care of pH meters, and particularly of the elec-
trode, is essential for maintaining the accuracy and precision
required for pH measurements and increases the longevity of
the equipment. Maintenance includes adhering to the manufac-
turer's instructions for the use and care of the pH instrument
system, routine electrode cleaning, reconditioning, and storage
requirements. As always, follow the manufacturer’s instruc-
tions for the specific type of electrode in use.
pH-meter and electrode performance is required to be
checked before each water-quality field trip and at each
field site.
3.1 	Electrode Care and Cleaning
USGS field personnel should integrate the following
guidance for the care and cleaning of pH electrodes into their
routine field-measurement procedures.
• Never handle the glass bulb with bare fingers. Oily film
or scratches on the bulb will interfere with the design
characteristics of the glass bulb membrane and affect
pH measurements.
• Inspect the electrode and electrode cable for:
• cut or frayed cable(s)
• broken connectors and mismatched or missing parts
• a visibly scratched or broken glass bulb, cracked
electrode body, and broken or damaged internal
electrodes (reference and measurement electrodes)
• a visibly contaminated reference junction
• low filling solution
• Periodically remove and replace the filling solution
• Gel-filled electrodes do not require filling and typically
require less maintenance than liquid-filled electrodes.
• Do not store gel-filled electrodes in low-ionic-
strength water, including DIW, even temporarily,
as ions will leach from the gel into the dilute water,
causing dilution of the filling gel and errors in pH

Probe cleaning
Coating of the pH bulb can lead to erroneous readings including shortened span (slope).
The type of coating will determine the cleaning technique. Soft coatings can be removed
by vigorous stirring or by the use of a squirt bottle. Organic chemical, or hard coatings,
should be chemically removed using a light bleach solution. If cleaning does not restore
performance, reconditioning may be tried. Do not use a brush or abrasive materials
on the pH probe.
How often do you need
to recalibrate a pH probe?
Because every use case is different, there is no set schedule for recalibration.
If you are using your probe in a fish tank, a hydroponic system or any environment that
has generally weak levels of acids and bases you will only need to recalibrate your probe
once per year for the first two years. After that every ~six months.
If you are using the pH probe in batch chemical manufacturing, industrial process,
or in a solution that is known to have strong acids and bases, then calibration should be
done monthly or in extreme cases after each batch.

modern pH meters automatically compensate for temperature

regularly with buffers equilibrated to the environmental-
sample temperatures to verify the readings. If the pH of the
buffers checked at the field site at ±10 °C of the temperature of
the environmental sample is more than ±0.05 pH unit different

meter and electrode should be recalibrated at a temperature
that is ±10 °C of the field-measurement temperature.
For multiparameter sondes that will be deployed for
continuous measurements in the field in a range of conditions,
the recommended procedure is to calibrate in the laboratory
and then conduct checks in the field at ambient tempera-

may be necessary if the initial check is more than ±0.05 pH

generally apply whenever a pH instrument system is to be
calibrated. Because calibration and operating procedures can
differ with the instrument system, check the manufacturer’s
recommended calibration procedures and calibration buffer
solution requirements. Modern pH meters typically compen-

When using these instruments, follow the manufacturer’s
calibration instructions and the more general instructions in
the following procedures—do not take shortcuts.
• Before each field trip and site visit, check pH-meter/
electrode logbook records for electrode performance.
Remember—any noted calibration slope of less
than 95 percent or greater than 101 percent indicates
probable electrode deterioration. If the slope is outside

should be cleaned, reconditioned, or replaced, and the
new electrode calibrated. If a liquid-filled electrode is

6.0 	Quality Assurance/Quality Control
for Measurements of pH
Field measurements, like all measurements of water
quality, require quality assurance to validate the accuracy
and precision of the data. For measurement of pH, quality
assurance includes documentation of meter calibration and
performance, proficiency testing of technicians, collection and
measurement of replicate samples to estimate variability, and
timely review of results to validate the data.
Replicate samples for quality assurance of pH measure-
ments are collected on a schedule specified in the project
data-management plan. Replicates for pH measurement should
be collected at least annually, and more frequently if needed.
Replicates in the field can be sequential, whereby multiple
samples are collected in the field and measured for pH, or can
be concurrent, whereby the pH of a water sample is mea-
sured and measured again after the instrument is checked and
recalibrated if needed. Replicate data are used to document
the precision of pH measurements in the field and to verify the
stability of the meter and probe.
Another check for pH measurements is to send a split
sample to the USGS National Water-Quality Laboratory
(NWQL) to compare its pH to that measured in the field.
Changes in temperature, gas composition, and redox condi-
tions could cause changes in chemistry, but this check can
still provide useful information about the stability of the water
quality of the sample.
USGS field personnel are required to participate in the
National Field Quality Assurance (NFQA) program. This
program, conducted annually by the USGS Quality Systems
Branch (QSB), provides blind samples for measurement of
pH, specific conductance, and alkalinity to field personnel for
testing. Field personnel measure the NFQA samples during
their regular sampling routine and can compare their results
with most probable values. When measurements are outside
established control limits, the tests are repeated, possible
reasons for the errors are investigated, and the technicians are
retrained to improve their techniques.
Results of measurements made on quality-control
samples are stored in the USGS National Water Information
System (NWIS) database.

unit at 25 °C) of the response expected according
to the theoretical Nernst equation (Busenberg and
Plummer, 1987).
• When measuring pH buffers, note whether stabilization
of the electrode requires more than 2 to 3 minutes.
Slow response times may indicate reduced electrode
performance or a clogged reference junction.
For routine cleaning of the pH electrode:
Electrodes must be kept clean and the reference junction
must be flowing freely to obtain accurate pH measurements.
Because a variety of electrodes is available, check the manu-
facturer’s instructions for specific tips and precautions.
• Before and after each use, rinse the electrode body
thoroughly, using only DIW.
• Do not wipe or wick moisture from electrodes with
paper towels or other paper-based wipes, as they can
scratch the glass bulb membrane. Wiping the elec-
trode body with paper also may cause a static charge
(polarization) on the exterior of the pH electrode,
which likewise can adversely affect the pH measure-
ment. Gently shaking electrodes to remove drops of
liquid is recommended. To prepare an electrode for
measurement, rinse it with the solution to be measured
by slowly pouring a small amount of the sample or
buffer to be measured over the electrode. Then place
the electrode into the vessel containing the sample or
buffer, remove the electrode, and dispose of the sample
or buffer. Repeat this process for a total of three times
prior to each pH measurement. To measure the pH
of the sample, add fresh sample or buffer to the same
vessel and then place the electrode directly into the
measurement vessel.
• If using a liquid-filled electrode that has been in a
storage solution for a long time (typically weeks to
months), uncap the fill hole and suspend the electrode
in the air for about 15 minutes. This procedure will
allow the filling solution to flush residual storage
solution through the porous reference junction and
thoroughly wet the junction.
• Soak the electrode (whether gel- or liquid-filled) in
0.1-M HCl for 30 minutes. This procedure removes
many of the solid precipitates that may be fouling the
reference junction. Thoroughly rinse the electrode with
DIW before using or storing.
• If the electrode is contaminated with oil or grease, soak
it in 0.5-percent mild liquid dishwashing detergent
solution for 3 minutes. Thoroughly rinse the electrode
with DIW before using or storing.
• For cleaning bacterial contaminants, soak the electrode
in a dilute (1:10 volume per volume) solution of bleach
(sodium hypochlorite) for 30 minutes. Thoroughly
rinse the electrode with DIW before using or storing.

-- 18 of 32 --4.0 	Calibration of the pH Instrument System 	11
have an isopotential point at pH 7 (the pH at which e.m.f. is
equal to 0 mV). Most modern pH meters are equipped with
ATC, which compensates for the temperature dependence of
the standard buffers. The Nernst equation gives the expected
(theoretical) response potential of the pH buffer at the specific
temperature of the calibration (Hem, 1989), and after calibra-
tion most meters report the calibration slope as a percentage
of the Nernstian theoretical slope. To successfully calibrate
pH instrumentation, (1) the meter and pH electrode must be
functioning properly, (2) the system must be calibrated with
pH buffers so the pH of the solution being measured is within
the calibrated range, and (3) the temperature of the pH buffers
during calibration needs be stable and similar to (within 10 °C
of) the temperature of the solution being measured.
A properly working pH system has—
• new or adequately charged batteries
• a thermistor that functions properly and accurately
measures the temperature
• a pH electrode with an accurate Nernstian response
(slope of 95–101 percent of the theoretical
Nernstian slope)
• an isopotential point near pH 7
• a quick response time (1–2 minutes) in standard
buffer solutions.
Accurate measurement of the pH of environmental
samples requires calibration with pH buffers that bracket the
pH of the sample. Before the pH instrument system is cali-
brated, it is useful to estimate (or anticipate from historical
site data, if available) the pH and conductivity of the waters to
be encountered at the field sites. If no data are available from
which to estimate sample pH, then pH indicator paper can
be used onsite as a gross indicator of the pH of the site, but
under no circumstances should a pH value from indica-
tor paper be recorded as the site pH. A two- or three-point
calibration can be performed. Most manufacturers use a linear
calibration curve for all calibrations (including multipoint
calibrations). For most modern meters, a two-point calibration,
typically with buffers selected from pH 10.01, 7.00, 4.01, or
1.68, is recommended. pH meters that use either a point-to-
point calibration or a nonlinear function are not recommended.
Follow the manufacturer’s instructions with respect to recom-
mended buffers and the sequence of buffer calibration.
Examples: When measuring pH in a stream—
• If pH values are expected to be between 7 and 8,
then the standard pH-7 and pH-10.01 buffers (at a
minimum) should be selected.
• If pH values are expected to be less than 7, then the
standard pH-7 and pH-4.01 buffers (at a minimum)
should be selected.
For the two examples above, a three-point calibration
using pH-4.01, -7.00, and -10.01 buffers could also be used to
allow measurement of a larger range of pH.
The pH of a solution changes with temperature, and most
modern pH meters automatically compensate for temperature

measurements made in samples. However, electrodes may not

Step 4. Recheck instrument calibration.
Check the stability of the pH meter and electrode in the
field by measuring the pH of the buffer whose pH is nearest
to that of the samples. If the pH of the buffer differs by more
than 0.05 pH units from the certified value at the measured
temperature (table 6.4–3), recalibrate the pH system and then
remeasure the pH of the sample.
5.2 	Measurement of pH in Waters with Low
Specific Conductance
Accurate and precise measurement of pH in low-specific-
conductance waters (less than 100 μS/cm) is challenging
because (1) the water is not sufficiently conductive to complete
the electrical circuit and allow for a stable pH reading using
a combination pH electrode, (2) differences in ionic strength
between the sample and buffers are large, and (3) the potential
of the liquid junction is larger than normal. Modern reference
junctions are designed to decrease the effects of low specific
conductance, but may not always produce the desired accuracy
for measurements of pH. Low-resistance glass pH electrodes
or reference junctions with a fast, continuous leak rate can
be used to make accurate measurements of pH in low-ionic-
strength waters; however, because these electrodes are expen-
sive, generally are not designed for fieldwork, and only work
well in dilute waters, they do not replace traditional electrodes.
Some methods recommend calibrating with low-ionic-strength
buffers to minimize liquid junction potential errors, but these
buffers are easily contaminated and should be avoided in
field settings.
The recommended method allows for using normal
pH field electrodes and standard pH buffers (table 6.4–3)
by adding a small amount of potassium chloride (KCl) to a
subsample of water to increase the specific conductance by
approximately 150 μS/cm. Increasing the specific conduc-
tance by this amount has little effect on the hydrogen ion
activity coefficient; the pH is expected to be affected by less
than 0.01 pH units (Busenberg and Plummer, 1987). It is first
recommended to determine the pH by using the procedures
described in section 5.1. If the sample pH does not stabilize,
and the specific conductance is less than 100 μS/cm, then the
following procedure is recommended:
1. 	Before going to the field, prepare small glass vials
containing 20 milligrams (mg) of dry potassium chlo-
ride (KCl—crystalline, American Chemical Society-
certified). Prepare more vials than the expected number
of pH measurements. (Note: Addition of other salts [for
example, sodium chloride] also will increase the specific
conductance, but KCl is recommended to minimize
effects on the liquid junction potential.)
2. 	At the sample site, fill a 250-mL polyethylene bottle with
raw sample water. Immediately transfer 20 mg KCl to
the sample solution, cap the solution to minimize trans-
fer of gases, and gently swirl the bottle to dissolve the
KCl. Maintain the sample at ambient temperature. This
procedure will increase the specific conductance of the
sample by approximately 150 μS/cm.

Step 3. Measure pH
1. 	Set up the pH instrumentation at the sampling site.
2. 	Measurements of pH in a sample vessel such as a
beaker or other container—
a. 	Fill the sample vessel with sufficient sample to
ensure that the electrode reference junction can be
fully immersed without submerging the fill hole,
taking care not to aerate the sample. Use only clean
measurement vessels.
b. 	First and second rinse in sample solution—
Immerse the electrode and thermistor in the sample;
swirl to rinse the electrode body from above the
reference junction to the bottom of the bulb. Discard
the sample appropriately. Be careful not to submerge
the fill hole. Repeat this step for a total of two times.
c. 	Third rinse—Pour the next aliquot of sample into
the vessel and immerse and swirl the electrode
in the sample for 1 minute. Discard the waste
sample appropriately.
d. 	Refill the vessel with another aliquot of sample—
Place the electrode in the sample and swirl gently
to equilibrate, making sure that no bubbles are
trapped against the pH bulb and the glass bulb of the
electrode does not contact the sides or bottom of the
measurement vessel.
e. 	Stop swirling and allow the sample to be quiescent
before recording pH.
3. 	Measurements in a flow-through cell or
chamber system—
a. 	Connect the flow-through cell with probes installed
to the pumping system and begin pumping to purge.
b. 	Allow the system to purge and the sensors to equili-
brate with the water for 5 minutes or more.
c. 	Stop the pump or divert flow from the cell to allow
the water in the chamber to become quiescent to
record the final measurement of pH.
4. 	In situ measurements of pH—
a. 	Rinse the electrode and thermistor thoroughly with
DIW and then with the sample by pouring directly
over the electrode and thermistor and appropriately
discarding the rinse.
b. 	Place the electrode into the water. If a single-
parameter pH instrument with refillable electrode is
being used, be sure to keep the fill hole above the
water surface.
c. 	If the water body being measured in situ is not
moving, gently swirl the electrode and allow
the electrode and water to equilibrate for at least
1 minute and until the reading stabilizes.
d. 	Stop swirling and allow the sample to become
quiescent to record pH. Conditions of flow over the
electrode should be recorded if the water is moving.
5. 	Record the final pH, millivolts (if available), and
temperature under quiescent sample conditions if pos-
sible when the reading stabilizes.
• A pH value is assumed to be stable when three to
five readings made at regularly spaced intervals are
within ±0.1 pH units. If measurements continue to
fluctuate outside the acceptable range, continue to
monitor, or, if site conditions are demonstrably vari-
able (degassing, rapid thermal changes due to mix-
ing of water at depth), select the median of three or
more measurements made within about 60 seconds
as the value to record.
• If the pH measurement does not stabilize and con-
tinually drifts in one direction, record the final mea-

Not a dumb question — and no, the guidance says not to do that. You should never insert the electrode into a stock buffer bottle: "Do not insert an electrode or other material into a bottle containing stock buffer solution—always pour the buffer into a separate container and discard the solution after use" 【6】. The reason given is contamination — a wet or contaminated electrode placed into the solution can contaminate or dilute it 【6】.

Instead, pour the buffer into a separate, dedicated beaker for calibration 【3】, and rinse the electrode with the buffer before measuring 【6】. Also note buffers that have been poured out shouldn't go back — they're discarded after use 【6】.

turns.question: The decanted bottles live in the truck. How long can I keep using those before I throw them out?
turns.answer:
The guidance doesn't give a shelf life for decanted buffer in the field — but it does say to refresh them each trip: "Buffers that have been transferred to a secondary bottle for use while in the field should be refreshed before every field trip" 【10】.

A few related points from the same source:

- Never pour used buffer back into the stock bottle 【3】.
- Label secondary bottles with the buffer's pH value, lot number, and expiration date, and don't use buffers past their expiration date 【10】.
- Protect buffers from wide temperature swings — "Never expose buffers to extreme heat or freezing temperatures. If buffers experience these conditions, their pH values can no longer be assumed to be valid and they should be discarded appropriately" 【6】. A truck cab in summer or winter could easily do that.

So the practical answer from the documents: refresh before every field trip rather than trying to stretch them, and discard anything expired or heat/freeze-exposed.

2.3 	Standard pH Buffer Solutions
Standard pH buffer solutions (buffers) are ionic solutions
that are used to calibrate the pH meter and electrodes. Buffers
maintain constant pH values (at a single temperature) because
of their ability to resist changes to the specific pH value for
which they are produced. However, the pH of solutions is
affected by temperature, because the calibration slope (which
is related to the Nernst equation) and the isopotential point
change with temperature. Modern pH meters are typically
calibrated with pH buffers having well-known pH-temper-
ature correlations; quality-assured and National Institute of
Standards and Technology- (NIST) traceable pH buffers are
available from USGS One-Stop1. Most pH meters recognize
the e.m.f. range of certain pH buffers (commonly pH 1.68,
4.01, 7.00, and 10.01 buffers) and are able to automatically
compensate for temperature during calibration. Verify that
the buffers you are using are NIST-traceable, that the values
are recognized correctly by the meter, and that the buffers are
compatible with the ATC for your meter. Consult the manu-
facturer’s manual to be sure that the meter will adjust the
expected value of the buffer for the temperature measured. The
user may be responsible for entering the temperature-adjusted
buffer pH value into the meter for calibration from a chart or
the meter may automatically generate a temperature-adjusted
pH value for the buffer.
Measurements of pH are only as accurate as the buffers
used to calibrate the meter and electrodes.
The commonly used pH buffer solutions and their corre-
sponding pH values from 0 to 90 °C are shown in table 6.4–3.
The pH buffers 1.68, 4.01, and 10.01 are primary standards
(pH values determined by using the standard hydrogen-gas
electrode). Their compositions are typically similar for various
manufacturers; therefore, their variations in pH with tem-
perature are well known. The pH-7.00 buffer is a secondary
standard (pH values determined by interpolation to primary
standards) and its composition (and therefore pH dependence
on temperature) may differ with the manufacturer. However,
the pH-7.00 buffer is typically made either from potassium
dihydrogen phosphate plus sodium hydroxide or from potas-
sium dihydrogen phosphate plus sodium hydrogen phosphate;
the pH values of both buffer formulations are comparable to
within 0.02 pH units from 0 to 90 °C.

3.0 	Maintenance and Preparation of
pH Instruments
Proper care of pH meters, and particularly of the elec-
trode, is essential for maintaining the accuracy and precision
required for pH measurements and increases the longevity of
the equipment. Maintenance includes adhering to the manufac-
turer's instructions for the use and care of the pH instrument
system, routine electrode cleaning, reconditioning, and storage
requirements. As always, follow the manufacturer’s instruc-
tions for the specific type of electrode in use.
pH-meter and electrode performance is required to be
checked before each water-quality field trip and at each
field site.
3.1 	Electrode Care and Cleaning
USGS field personnel should integrate the following
guidance for the care and cleaning of pH electrodes into their
routine field-measurement procedures.
• Never handle the glass bulb with bare fingers. Oily film
or scratches on the bulb will interfere with the design
characteristics of the glass bulb membrane and affect
pH measurements.
• Inspect the electrode and electrode cable for:
• cut or frayed cable(s)
• broken connectors and mismatched or missing parts
• a visibly scratched or broken glass bulb, cracked
electrode body, and broken or damaged internal
electrodes (reference and measurement electrodes)
• a visibly contaminated reference junction
• low filling solution
• Periodically remove and replace the filling solution
• Gel-filled electrodes do not require filling and typically
require less maintenance than liquid-filled electrodes.
• Do not store gel-filled electrodes in low-ionic-
strength water, including DIW, even temporarily,
as ions will leach from the gel into the dilute water,
causing dilution of the filling gel and errors in pH

manufacturer for that buffer.

sensor is required to be performed at least annually
(NFM A6.1). Most single-analyte pH meters use a
thermistor built into the electrode. Multiparameter
instruments typically have the temperature sensor
in a different part of the instrument system than the
pH electrode.
• The pH instrumentation should be calibrated daily
and recalibrated if a check of either of the two pH
buffers nearest to the pH of the sample at a temperature
that is ± 10 °C of the sample deviates by more than
± 0.05 pH units.
• The isopotential point is the characteristic pH where
the e.m.f. is equal to 0 mV. Most modern pH electrodes
are designed to have an isopotential point at or near
pH=7. Test the electrode when it is new by placing it
in pH-7.00 buffer and record the voltage. Repeat this
test regularly and verify that the value is ±15 mV of
the original value. If the isopotential point is more than
±15 mV of the original value, clean, recondition, or
replace the electrode.
Do not use pH buffers that have exceeded their date of
expiration. Buffers that have been transferred to a second-
ary bottle for use while in the field should be refreshed

4.1 	Calibration Procedure
The following calibration procedure is expected to yield
accurate sample-pH measurements for waters with specific
conductance less than 60,000 μS/cm, temperatures from 0 to
90 °C, and pH in the range from 1.68 to 10. Standard buffer
solutions and combination pH electrode can be appropri-

of environmental waters that is within these environmental
ranges. Studies of waters with conditions that fall outside
the ranges described above may require pH calibration and
measurement modifications.

and pH Electrode used for Sample Measurement
or an Alkalinity Titration

the pH meter and electrode in a controlled environment

pH measurements between 4.0 and 9.5. Electrodes may
not behave ideally, however, and this feature should be
tested regularly with measurements on buffers equili-
brated to ambient field temperatures.

The pH of a solution changes with temperature, and most
modern pH meters automatically compensate for temperature
differences between the buffers used for calibration and the
measurements made in samples. However, electrodes may not
behave ideally and this feature should be tested regularly. Cali-

can be accomplished by placing the buffers in a mesh bag and
equilibrating them to the temperature of the water at the sam-
pling location before calibration. However, for most sampling
situations, where the temperature of the water is between 5 and
35 °C and the pH is between 4.0 and 9.5, the recommended
procedure is to calibrate the meter in the more controlled
environment of the office laboratory, and then allow the meter
to compensate for temperature differences at the sampling site.
Again, the accuracy of field measurements should be checked
regularly with buffers equilibrated to the environmental-
sample temperatures to verify the readings. If the pH of the
buffers checked at the field site at ±10 °C of the temperature of
the environmental sample is more than ±0.05 pH unit different
from the value the buffer should return at that temperature, the
meter and electrode should be recalibrated at a temperature
that is ±10 °C of the field-measurement temperature.
For multiparameter sondes that will be deployed for
continuous measurements in the field in a range of conditions,
the recommended procedure is to calibrate in the laboratory
and then conduct checks in the field at ambient tempera-
tures to verify the accuracy of the readings. Recalibration
may be necessary if the initial check is more than ±0.05 pH
unit different from the value the buffer should return. If the
measurement temperature is more than ±10 °C different from
the laboratory calibration temperature, checks in the field are
more likely to fail and recalibration may be necessary.
The following guidelines and standard procedures
generally apply whenever a pH instrument system is to be
calibrated. Because calibration and operating procedures can
differ with the instrument system, check the manufacturer’s
recommended calibration procedures and calibration buffer
solution requirements. Modern pH meters typically compen-
sate for buffer temperatures automatically during calibration.
When using these instruments, follow the manufacturer’s
calibration instructions and the more general instructions in
the following procedures—do not take shortcuts.
• Before each field trip and site visit, check pH-meter/
electrode logbook records for electrode performance.
Remember—any noted calibration slope of less
than 95 percent or greater than 101 percent indicates
probable electrode deterioration. If the slope is outside
the acceptable range (95–101 percent), the electrode
should be cleaned, reconditioned, or replaced, and the
new electrode calibrated. If a liquid-filled electrode is
being used, try reconditioning it (section 3.2) in the
laboratory before replacing it with a new electrode.

Probe cleaning
Coating of the pH bulb can lead to erroneous readings including shortened span (slope).
The type of coating will determine the cleaning technique. Soft coatings can be removed
by vigorous stirring or by the use of a squirt bottle. Organic chemical, or hard coatings,
should be chemically removed using a light bleach solution. If cleaning does not restore
performance, reconditioning may be tried. Do not use a brush or abrasive materials
on the pH probe.
How often do you need
to recalibrate a pH probe?
Because every use case is different, there is no set schedule for recalibration.
If you are using your probe in a fish tank, a hydroponic system or any environment that
has generally weak levels of acids and bases you will only need to recalibrate your probe
once per year for the first two years. After that every ~six months.
If you are using the pH probe in batch chemical manufacturing, industrial process,
or in a solution that is known to have strong acids and bases, then calibration should be
done monthly or in extreme cases after each batch.

If problems persist during calibration of a liquid-filledelectrode, or if there is reason to doubt that the electrode is in
good working condition, check the manufacturer’s instructions
for testing and reconditioning the electrode. Reconditioning
procedures should be implemented if the electrode’s slope
response has deteriorated to less than 95 percent or greater
than 101 percent, if the meter no longer recognizes the pH
buffers because of shifting of the isopotential point, or if the
response time is longer than expected. Document the date,
serial number, and action in the pH-meter/electrode logbook if

removing the filling solution is to wick it out with

The guidance doesn't give a shelf life for decanted buffer in the field — but it does say to refresh them each trip: "Buffers that have been transferred to a secondary bottle for use while in the field should be refreshed before every field trip" 【10】.

A few related points from the same source:

- Never pour used buffer back into the stock bottle 【3】.
- Label secondary bottles with the buffer's pH value, lot number, and expiration date, and don't use buffers past their expiration date 【10】.
- Protect buffers from wide temperature swings — "Never expose buffers to extreme heat or freezing temperatures. If buffers experience these conditions, their pH values can no longer be assumed to be valid and they should be discarded appropriately" 【6】. A truck cab in summer or winter could easily do that.

So the practical answer from the documents: refresh before every field trip rather than trying to stretch them, and discard anything expired or heat/freeze-exposed.
